title: Research Bite #80: Understanding Verbal Probability Expressions
author: Craig Barton
summary: In this weekly Research Bite, Craig Barton breaks down a study by Ran Peleg, Rosalyn Hyde and Christian Bokhove on how secondary students turn probability words such as likely or rarely into numbers. The study asked 184 students in five English schools to place 29 probability words on a slider from 0 to 100 percent. Students disagreed most on extreme words like certain and impossible and on words like very likely, and agreed most on words near 50 percent. Older students gave more extreme and more consistent answers, and there was almost no gender difference. Barton's central takeaway is that a phrase like very likely may not carry the meaning the teacher intends, since students averaged 74 percent where scientific guidance treats it as above 90 percent. His classroom implications include attaching numbers to words, using the study's task as a mini-whiteboard starter, being careful with possible, and agreeing a short shared list of probability words across a department. He closes with the study's limits, including a one-off questionnaire and unrecorded language backgrounds.
points: Students interpret probability words less strongly than adults and disagree widely, so a teacher's very likely may land well below what was meant.
Pairing a word with a percentage or fraction removes ambiguity when the exact chance matters.
A quick mini-whiteboard task asking students to write a percentage for words like unlikely and probable exposes the spread in a class before shared meanings are set.
The word possible was read as roughly an even chance, so teachers should say plainly when they mean it could happen but probably will not.
Departments can agree one or two words per probability group and use them consistently across maths and science.
quotes: Uncertain scientific information is often communicated with words such as “likely” or “rarely” in place of numbers. This study asked how secondary school students in England turn those words into numbers.
Students disagreed most on words at the extremes (”certain”, “impossible”) and on words for events that are more likely than not (”very likely”, “usually”).
Students in this study read probability words less strongly than adults do, and they disagreed with each other a lot. “Certain” averaged 83% and “impossible” averaged 13%.
If you tell a class that an outcome is “very likely”, add a percentage or a fraction so they know how strong a claim you are making.
Spend lesson time agreeing what probability words mean. The authors point out that teachers rarely teach these words because they presume students already know them.

Students placed it at about 53%, close to “maybe”, while “impossible” sat near the bottom of the scale. So a student who hears “it’s possible the experiment will fail” may take that as roughly an even chance.
Choosing one or two words per group and using them consistently across maths and science gives students fewer meanings to guess at.
This was a one-off questionnaire in five schools in the South of England, and the authors had limited means of checking students engaged.
